title: Whatever is lovely (Philippians 4:8–9)
hookLine: whatever is true, noble, pure, lovely: think on these things

cards: An argument between strangers. A crime two states away. Someone's perfect kitchen.
An ad that knew what you'd been thinking about. Ten minutes on a phone, and all of that went in. None of it was chosen, exactly.
It just arrived, and it stayed. Paul has just promised the Philippians a peace that will guard their hearts and minds. Now he tells them what to let through the gate.

teach.b: Here it is in the King James Bible, worth hearing slowly: "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things."
Six whatsoevers, then two ifs. Honest, in the old English, means honorable, worthy of respect. Of good report: things that speak well.
The word for lovely is an unusual one.
It means pleasing, winsome, the kind of thing that makes you want to come closer.

And a surprise: some of these words, virtue especially, were also at home among the Greek moral philosophers. Paul borrows the vocabulary that thoughtful people in a Greek city already used about the good life.
He seems to say: whatever is genuinely good, wherever you find it, take it in. Then the verb: think on these things.
The Greek means to reckon, to count up, to dwell on deliberately, the same verb Paul used when he said he didn't count himself to have arrived. This isn't wishful thinking or ignoring what's wrong.

It's choosing what you keep turning over. And he doesn't leave it as thinking: "Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you."

teach.h: THINK ON THEM. THEN DO THEM.
teach.b: Think on them, then do them.
Yesterday, the peace of God. Today, the God of peace.

how: Some Christians use Philippians 4:8 as a test for what they read, watch and talk about.

o: courage and strength shown by soldiers in battle
keeping every rule so no one can blame you
goodness of character, a word the philosophers used too

s: Paul's list borrows words Greek philosophers used
virtue especially was a key word of Greek moral teaching.
in the old English it meant honorable, worthy of respect.
Paul says only to think about these things, not to act
the next line says: learned, received, heard and seen in me, do.

games.q: your mind keeps returning to an argument you saw online. using Paul's list, what do you do?
o: keep replaying it so you're ready to win next time.
choose something true and lovely and dwell on that instead.
games.why: "whatsoever things are lovely... think on these things." not denial: a deliberate choice of what to keep turning over.

practice: Pick one thing from the last few days that was true, or good, or simply lovely: a child's laugh, light on a wall, someone keeping a promise, a song.
Stay with it on purpose, the place, the sound, the color, and when your mind drifts back to a worry, bring it gently back to the lovely thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Virtue. One of Paul's words for what to let into the mind, at home among the Greek philosophers too: the truly good, true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report.

orig.note: Greek: lovely, pleasing, winsome. it is built on phil-, the root of friendly love.

carryVoice: Your line: think on these things. True, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report. Day six hundred sixty-seven, complete.
